why: Public keys whose PRIVATE half was published by apps/lexitar/migrations/0002_seed_migrated_accounts.sql, wrapped under a PBKDF2 KEK over a short human string. MEASURED 2026-10-06, because the first version of this sentence claimed more than was true: exactly ONE of the three account keys unwraps with a literal printed in that file — the provider's, under its 4-character slug — and it is the worst one, because the provider holds a recovery envelope on every prod vault. The two owner keys are wrapped under a passphrase that appears nowhere in the published file, almost certainly the pre-2026-08-31 slug the G1 rename replaced, which survives only in plover-code's private history. They are listed here regardless and that is not caution: a KEK derived from a human first name falls to a wordlist, so the right reading is a clone-only read for the provider's reach and a trivially-brute-forced one for the other two. A DEK wrapped to any of these is a DEK anyone holding a clone of this repository between 2026-09-14 and 2026-10-06 can unwrap. scripts/vault-rekey.ts refuses to mint an envelope to any of them, which is what makes the rotation order an invariant rather than something an operator has to remember: replace the keypair FIRST, then rotate the DEK.
safeToCommit: A thumbprint is a hash of a PUBLIC key. It is not key material, it is not a secret, and it cannot be reversed into one. It is recorded here because the file that published these keys is rewritten in Phase 4 and the list would otherwise be unrecoverable. The accountId beside it is a different claim and needs its own. Since migrations/0002_seed_migrated_accounts.sql was rewritten synthetic on 2026-10-06 these are the only real account identifiers this repository tracks, and Phase 5 returns the repository to public. They stay anyway, and the reason is that an identifier here resolves to nothing: the D1 database and R2 bucket it indexes are unreachable without a Cloudflare API token, this file carries no name, no email address and no health fact beside it, and as of 2026-10-07 every key it names is replaced and dead in BOTH stores -- so the id addresses a principal whose published key opens no vault in either. What would genuinely not be publishable is one of these ids paired with a person, and that pairing exists in no file of this repository.
accountIdsDecidedAt: 2026-10-07 -- Phase 4(l). Both fields stay, and the keyed field could not have been changed even had the paragraph above gone the other way. rekeyScope (src/lib/vault-rekey-plan.ts:104-107) builds its map from accountId, and that file's docblock at :70-102 is the measurement rather than the preference: a vault envelope records only principal_account_id and the SENDER's ephemeral public key, never which recipient key it was wrapped to. So once keypair:replace has run, a thumbprint-keyed scope reports every vault as needing nothing while every envelope on it is still openable by a published private key -- a silent no-op in the one ordering the remediation actually runs in, which is worse than a refusal. Dropping accountId empties the scope rather than narrowing it. The remediation plan's Phase 4 report carried the opposite instruction, to drop accountId and re-key rekeyScope on thumbprint once prod was re-keyed; prod was re-keyed on 2026-10-07 and that instruction is withdrawn there and here.
algorithm: RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint: base64url(SHA-256(JSON of crv,kty,x,y with sorted keys and no whitespace)), unpadded.
rolesCorrectedAt: 2026-10-06 — the provider and one owner were swapped. role is printed and never branched on (the refusal keys on thumbprint, rekeyScope on accountId), so nothing behaved differently — but the Finding section of the remediation plan reasoned about blast radius by role, and it named the wrong account id while reaching the right conclusion.
